claim: In the 2023-24 Civil Rights Data Collection, 19 school districts in states that prohibit corporal punishment reported students struck, totalling 418 students; 380 of those come from one New Jersey district whose ratio of instances to students, 4.4, is roughly three times that of any state where corporal punishment is lawful.

sources.title: 2023-24 Civil Rights Data Collection, SCH/Corporal Punishment.csv
sources.publisher: US Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights

body:
Computed by this project from the same file as the national figure; see `data/crdc/2023-24/SOURCE.md`.

## Why these numbers are almost certainly not corporal punishment

**One district is 91% of it.** Salem City School District, New Jersey, reports 380 students and 1,655
instances across three schools. New Jersey has prohibited corporal punishment in its schools since
1867, the first state to do so.

**The ratio is wrong for paddling.** Instances per student in the states where corporal punishment is
lawful sit in a narrow band: Texas 1.6, Arkansas 1.4, Alabama 1.2, Mississippi 1.2. A paddled student
is typically paddled once or twice in a year. Salem City reports 4.4 instances per student, about
three times the highest lawful-state figure.

**The disability share is wrong too.** 89 of Salem City's 380 students, 23%, are students with
disabilities. In Mississippi the figure is 22 of 2,653, under 1%. A rate that far out of line is the
signature of a different practice being entered in this field.

Both patterns fit physical restraint or seclusion rather than corporal punishment: a small number of
students, each involved in repeated incidents, concentrated among students with disabilities. The CRDC
collects restraint and seclusion separately, and a district that files them in the wrong column
produces exactly this shape.

## The other eighteen

The remaining 38 students are spread across 18 districts and 14 of them report one or two students,
which is the ordinary single-cell noise of a collection this size. Three are not ordinary districts at
all but regional service agencies serving students with disabilities across member districts:
Northwest Educational Service District 189 in Washington, and two New York BOCES. That is again where
restraint and seclusion happen.

## What follows from this

The national total of 19,851 should be read as 19,471 in the states where the practice is lawful, plus
380 from one filing that does not behave like corporal punishment. Neither figure is corrected here:
the raw number is what the district filed and this project does not edit federal data. It is flagged,
and any ban-state district in `districts.csv` should be treated as a reporting question rather than a
scanning target until someone has asked the district what it filed.

None of this is a finding about what happened to any child in Salem City. It is a finding about a
number in a spreadsheet, and the way to resolve it is to ask the district, which nobody has yet.

body:
Black letter as posted by the ALI in April 2019 (Part II, Children in Schools; Chapter 8, Discipline and Order Maintenance; Topic 1; section 8.10, Use of Force to Control and Punish), first paragraph: "In a criminal proceeding or a civil suit alleging an intentional tort, the use of reasonable force by a teacher or other school authority with responsibility for the care and education of students is privileged if the school authority reasonably believes that the force is necessary to maintain order and safety in the school." Second paragraph as in the claim.

Comment c (page 145): "Where a broad and growing legal, medical, and social scientific consensus categorically rejects the propriety and efficacy of corporal punishment, corporal punishment cannot be said to be 'necessary.' Thus, application of the 'reasonable belief in necessity' requirement precludes application of the common-law privilege to corporal punishment." Comment c also says that "in both the school and family setting, there is a growing social scientific consensus that the use of corporal punishment is ineffective and potentially harmful to children." Comment a (page 143): "Where corporal punishment is still authorized by statute, this Restatement notes that the reasonableness contemplated in those statutes is increasingly out of step with trends in the law."

Status of the text. The PDF read here carries the footer "Tentative draft – not approved" because it was posted before the May 2019 Annual Meeting. claim: In Canadian Foundation for Children, Youth and the Law v. Canada (Attorney General), 2004 SCC 4, decided January 30, 2004, the Supreme Court of Canada read the words 'reasonable under the circumstances' in Criminal Code section 43 against the expert evidence and held that 'substantial societal consensus, supported by expert evidence and Canada's treaty obligations, indicates that corporal punishment by teachers is unreasonable', so that teachers 'may reasonably apply force to remove a child from a classroom or secure compliance with instructions, but not merely as corporal punishment.'

sources.title: Canadian Foundation for Children, Youth and the Law v. Canada (Attorney General), [2004] 1 S.C.R. 76, 2004 SCC 4 (reasons, PDF)
Case page

body:
Majority reasons by McLachlin C.J. The passages: paragraph 38, "Contemporary social consensus is that, while teachers may sometimes use corrective force to remove children from classrooms or secure compliance with instructions, the use of corporal punishment by teachers is not acceptable. Many school boards forbid the use of corporal punishment, and some provinces and territories have legislatively prohibited its use by teachers ... Section 43 will protect a teacher who uses reasonable, corrective force to restrain or remove a child in appropriate circumstances. Substantial societal consensus, supported by expert evidence and Canada's treaty obligations, indicates that corporal punishment by teachers is unreasonable." Paragraph 40, "Teachers may reasonably apply force to remove a child from a classroom or secure compliance with instructions, but not merely as corporal punishment." Paragraph 37 records the experts' agreement that corporal punishment of children under two and of teenagers, with objects, or to the head is harmful and "will not be reasonable." The statute was upheld for parents (minor corrective force of a transitory and trifling nature); the court narrowed it by interpretation rather than striking it. Dissents by Binnie, Arbour and Deschamps JJ. Use as the clearest example of a court reading a reasonableness standard against the evidence and removing teachers from it.

claim: Ala. Code section 16-28A-1 (Acts 1995, No. 95-539) gives teachers 'the authority and responsibility to use appropriate means of discipline up to and including corporal punishment as may be prescribed by the local board of education' and provides that 'so long as teachers follow approved policy in the exercise of their responsibility to maintain discipline in their classroom, such teacher shall be immune from civil or criminal liability'; the statute's only standard words are 'appropriate' and 'follow approved policy', with no reasonableness, necessity or excess language.

sources.title: Code of Alabama, section 16-28A-1, Legislative Findings
Code of Alabama, section 16-28A-5, Immunity for Other Authorized School Personnel

body:
Section 16-28A-1 in full: "It is the finding of the Alabama Legislature that the people of Alabama have two basic expectations of their public schools: (1) that students be allowed to learn in a safe classroom setting where order and discipline are maintained; and (2) that students learn at the level of their capabilities and achieve accordingly. ... The teacher in each classroom is expected to maintain order and discipline. Teachers are hereby given the authority and responsibility to use appropriate means of discipline up to and including corporal punishment as may be prescribed by the local board of education. So long as teachers follow approved policy in the exercise of their responsibility to maintain discipline in their classroom, such teacher shall be immune from civil or criminal liability. It shall be the responsibility of the local boards of education and the administrators employed by them to provide legal support to each teacher exercising his or her authority and responsibility to maintain order and discipline in his or her classroom as long as the teacher follows the local board of education's policy. ... Local school board authorities and school administrators providing such support shall be absolutely immune from civil and criminal liability for actions authorized or required by this section." Section 16-28A-5 extends the chapter to "principals, assistant principals and any other school personnel authorized to use corporal punishment under the policies and guidelines developed by the local board of education."

Reading: the immunity is conditioned entirely on policy compliance and on the word "appropriate," so the reasonableness and necessity limits come from the common law (Ingraham; Restatement (Second) of Torts section 147(2)) and from the board's own policy, which in Alabama usually says "reasonable."

body:
Text as enacted (the act prints the amended sections in full, so the quotation is of the statute, not a summary). Section 6-17-112(a)(1): "Except as provided under subdivision (a)(2) of this section, teachers and administrators in a school district that authorizes use of corporal punishment in the school district's written student discipline policy shall be immune from any civil liability for administering corporal punishment to students, provided only that the corporal punishment is administered in substantial compliance with the school district's written student discipline policy." (a)(2): "A teacher or administrator in a school district that authorizes use of corporal punishment in the school district's written student disciplinary policy is not immune from civil liability under subdivision (a)(1) of this section if the teacher or administrator uses corporal punishment on a child who is intellectually disabled, non-ambulatory, non-verbal, or autistic." Section 6-18-505(c)(1): "A teacher or school administrator in a school district that authorizes use of corporal punishment in the district's written student discipline policy may use corporal punishment, provided only that if the punishment is administered in accord with the district's written student discipline policy, on any pupil, except a child who is intellectually disabled, non-ambulatory, non-verbal, or autistic, in order to maintain discipline and order within the public schools." Section 6-17-1113(a)(2)(B) removes the School Worker Defense Program's cover for the same four categories.

Standard words: "substantial compliance" with written policy and "in order to maintain discipline and order"; no reasonableness or excess language in these subsections. The conditions in section 6-18-503(b)(1) recorded in data/states/AR.yaml (for cause, reasonable, after warning, in an administrator's presence) were not opened at a primary source on this date: the official Arkansas Code is served by a LexisNexis portal that put a CAPTCHA in front of the section page, and no later act was found to have changed that subsection. The portal's search view truncated the section there; the remaining requirements (a witness informed beforehand, a written explanation to the parent on request, and the exemption for a child whose parent files a physician's statement) are recorded in data/states/GA.yaml from an earlier read and were not re-read on this date because the portal's full-document view sits behind a CAPTCHA.

Such consent applies only to the school year in which it is given. No form of corporal punishment shall be administered to a student with an exceptionality as defined in R.S. 17:1942 or to a student who has been determined to be eligible for services under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and has an Individual Accommodation Plan." (B)(2) defines corporal punishment as "using physical force to discipline a student, with or without an object" including "hitting, paddling, striking, spanking, slapping, or any other physical force that causes pain or physical discomfort," and bars taping a student's mouth "regardless of parental consent." (B)(3)(a) excludes "the use of reasonable and necessary physical restraint of a student to protect the student or others from bodily harm." Subsection (C): "Should any teacher, principal, or administrator in the public school system be sued for damages ... it shall be the responsibility of the school board employing such teacher, principal, or administrator to provide such defendant with a legal defense to such suit ... Should any such teacher, principal, or administrator be cast in judgment for damages in such suit, it shall be the obligation of the school board employing such defendant to indemnify him fully against such judgment ... Nothing in this Section shall require a school board to indemnify a teacher, principal, or administrator against a judgment wherein there is a specific decree in the judgment that the action of the teacher, principal, or administrator was malicious, and willfully and deliberately intended to cause bodily harm." History line: Acts 1975, No. 559; 1988, No. 898; 2003, No. 732; 2017, No. 266; 2023, No. 268; 2024, No. 780; 2025, No. 479 (effective December 1, 2025).

Standard words: "reasonable disciplinary and corrective measures to maintain order," "reasonable and necessary physical restraint" (for the restraint exclusion), "malicious, and willfully and deliberately intended to cause bodily harm" (the indemnity exception). Louisiana is not an immunity statute but an indemnity one: the board pays, so the board carries the exposure.

claim: Miss. Code section 37-11-57(2), as amended by HB 1182 (2019), provides that 'corporal punishment administered in a reasonable manner ... does not constitute negligence or child abuse' and bars civil damages 'unless the court determines that the teacher, assistant teacher, principal or assistant principal acted in bad faith or with malicious purpose or in a manner exhibiting a wanton and willful disregard of human rights or safety', defining corporal punishment as 'the reasonable use of physical force or physical contact ... as may be necessary to maintain discipline, to enforce a school rule, for self-protection or for the protection of other students from disruptive students'; subsection (1) excepts 'excessive force or cruel and unusual punishment' and subsection (3) withholds immunity for any student with an IEP or Section 504 plan.

body:
Subsection (1): "Except in the case of excessive force or cruel and unusual punishment, a public school teacher, assistant teacher, principal, or an assistant principal acting within the course and scope of his employment shall not be liable for any action carried out in conformity with state or federal law or rules or regulations of the State Board of Education or the local school board or governing board of a charter school regarding the control, discipline, suspension and expulsion of students." Subsection (2): "Corporal punishment administered in a reasonable manner, or any reasonable action to maintain control and discipline of students taken by a public school teacher, assistant teacher, principal or assistant principal acting within the scope of his employment or function and in accordance with any state or federal laws or rules or regulations of the State Board of Education or the local school board or governing board of a charter school does not constitute negligence or child abuse. No public school teacher, assistant teacher, principal or assistant principal so acting shall be held liable in a suit for civil damages alleged to have been suffered by a student as a result of the administration of corporal punishment, or the taking of action to maintain control and discipline of a student, unless the court determines that the teacher, assistant teacher, principal or assistant principal acted in bad faith or with malicious purpose or in a manner exhibiting a wanton and willful disregard of human rights or safety. For the purposes of this subsection, 'corporal punishment' means the reasonable use of physical force or physical contact by a teacher, assistant teacher, principal or assistant principal, as may be necessary to maintain discipline, to enforce a school rule, for self-protection or for the protection of other students from disruptive students." Subsection (3) prohibits corporal punishment on any student with an IEP or a Section 504 plan and provides that "no school personnel shall be granted immunity from liability under subsection (2) of this section for the use of corporal punishment on a student with a disability." Effective July 1, 2019.

Standard words: "reasonable manner," "reasonable use of physical force ... as may be necessary," "excessive force," "bad faith or with malicious purpose." Mississippi's own definition builds necessity into the term "corporal punishment": force that is not necessary to maintain discipline is, by the statute's definition, not corporal punishment at all and gets no immunity. The current code text is served by a LexisNexis portal; the enrolled bill was used because it prints the section in full and no later amendment was found.

body:
Subsection 1 (opening): "The local board of education of each school district shall clearly establish a written policy of discipline, including the district's determination on the use of corporal punishment and the procedures in which punishment will be applied. ... No pupil shall be subject to corporal punishment procedures outlined in the discipline and corporal punishment policy without a parent or guardian being notified and providing written permission for the corporal punishment." Subsection 8: "Teachers and other authorized district personnel in public schools responsible for the care, supervision, and discipline of schoolchildren, including volunteers selected with reasonable care by the school district, shall not be civilly liable when acting in conformity with the established policies developed by each board, including but not limited to policies of student discipline ... Nothing in this section shall be construed to create a new cause of action against such school district, or to relieve the school district from liability for the negligent acts of such persons." Subsection 10 as quoted in the claim.

Standard words: "reasonable force," "reasonable manner," "in accordance with the local board of education's written policy," "in conformity with the established policies." The spanking clause itself carries no reasonableness word; its conditions are certificated personnel, a witness, and the parent's written permission. The reasonableness and necessity limits therefore come from the board's own policy (Missouri boards that permit it almost all say "reasonable") and from the common law.

claim: Texas Penal Code section 9.62 justifies an educator's non-deadly force only 'when and to the degree the actor reasonably believes the force is necessary to further the special purpose or to maintain discipline in a group'; Education Code section 22.0512 bars a district from disciplining an employee for force 'to the extent justified under Section 9.62' while preserving the district's power to enforce 'a policy relating to corporal punishment'; and section 37.0011 lets an educator use corporal punishment where the board's code of conduct permits it unless the parent 'has previously provided a written, signed statement prohibiting' it.

body:
Penal Code section 9.62 in full: "The use of force, but not deadly force, against a person is justified: (1) if the actor is entrusted with the care, supervision, or administration of the person for a special purpose; and (2) when and to the degree the actor reasonably believes the force is necessary to further the special purpose or to maintain discipline in a group." Education Code section 22.0512(a): "A professional employee of a school district may not be subject to disciplinary proceedings for the employee's use of physical force against a student to the extent justified under Section 9.62, Penal Code." Section 22.0512(c): "This section does not prohibit a school district from: (1) enforcing a policy relating to corporal punishment; or (2) notwithstanding Subsection (a), bringing a disciplinary proceeding against a professional employee of the district who violates the district policy relating to corporal punishment." Section 37.0011(a) defines corporal punishment as "the deliberate infliction of physical pain by hitting, paddling, spanking, slapping, or any other physical force used as a means of discipline," excluding athletic activity and authorized restraint; (b) to (d) set the opt-out.

Standard words: "reasonably believes the force is necessary" (Penal Code), "to the extent justified under Section 9.62" (Education Code). Texas is the one state in this set whose statute makes reasonable belief in necessity the explicit condition of the justification, in the Restatement's own terms. Texas Education Code section 22.0511 (immunity from civil liability for acts within the scope of duties involving judgment or discretion, with an exception for excessive force in discipline) was not re-read on this date and is not quoted here.

body:
Subsections (a) and (b) in full: "(a) Each board of trustees in each school district within the state may adopt rules for reasonable forms of punishment and disciplinary measures. Subject to such rules, teachers, principals, and superintendents in such district may impose reasonable forms of punishment and disciplinary measures for insubordination, disobedience, and other misconduct. (b) Teachers, principals and superintendents in each district shall be immune from civil and criminal liability in the exercise of reasonable corporal discipline of a student as authorized by board policy." Standard words: "reasonable," three times, and "as authorized by board policy." The statute grants immunity for reasonable corporal discipline; it does not itself authorize the practice, which is why a Wyoming board that has no corporal punishment policy leaves its staff with no immunity to claim.

claim: In Ingraham v. Wright (1977), a 5-4 Supreme Court held that the Eighth Amendment does not apply to corporal punishment in public schools and that due process does not require a hearing before paddling because state tort and criminal remedies suffice; it expressly left open whether excessive corporal punishment violates substantive due process.

Ingraham v. Wright

body:
Powell for the Court; White dissenting with Brennan, Marshall and Stevens. The Court did acknowledge a 'constitutionally protected liberty interest' in freedom from bodily punishment (at 674) and left the substantive due process question open (at 659 n.12), which is where fifty years of circuit litigation have run.

At 661-662 the Court states the common-law rule it left in place: teachers 'may impose reasonable but not excessive force to discipline a child,' privileging force a teacher 'reasonably believes to be necessary for (the child's) proper control, training, or education' (Restatement (Second) of Torts section 147(2)), with reasonableness judged by 'all of the circumstances,' including 'the availability of less severe but equally effective means of discipline' (section 150, comments c-e). See law-restatement-second-torts-147-150.

body:
Verbatim from the how-to-file page: "A complaint must ordinarily be filed within 180 days of the last act of discrimination. If your complaint involves matters that occurred longer ago than this and you are requesting a waiver, you will be asked to show good cause why you did not file your complaint within the 180-day period." and "Anyone may file a complaint. The person or organization filing the complaint need not be a victim of the alleged discrimination but may complain on behalf of another person or group." From the complaint-form page: "The complainant will be informed that the complaint will be closed if written consent is necessary in order to resolve the complaint and is not received within 20 calendar days of the date of the acknowledgement letter or the date the Consent Form is requested from the complainant." and "Where the person is a minor (under the age of 18) or a legally incompetent adult, the Consent Form must be signed by that person's parent or legal guardian." OCR has a variety of options for resolving complaints, including facilitated resolutions and investigations. claim: Restatement (Second) of Torts section 147(2) (1965) privileges a teacher's force only to the extent the teacher 'reasonably believes [it] to be necessary' for the child's 'proper control, training, or education', and section 150 comment d withholds the privilege 'to use a means to compel obedience if a less severe method appears likely to be equally effective'; Ingraham v. Wright listed 'the availability of less severe but equally effective means of discipline' among the reasonableness factors, citing section 150 comments c to e.

sources.title: Ingraham v. Wright, 430 U.S. 651, 661-662 (1977), quoting Restatement (Second) of Torts section 147(2) and citing section 150 comments c-e
In re Rodney C., 91 Misc. 2d 677, 398 N.Y.S.2d 511 (N.Y. Fam. Ct. 1977), quoting Restatement (Second) of Torts section 150 comments d and e
Sacks, State Actors Beating Children, 42 U.C. Davis L. Rev. 1165, 1174 n.34 (2009), paraphrasing the same passages

body:
The Restatement (Second) of Torts is not freely available online; the American Law Institute sells it. Every quotation here was read in a court opinion that quotes it, and the fact file records the words as the courts give them.

Ingraham, 430 U.S. at 661: "The prevalent rule in this country today privileges such force as a teacher or administrator 'reasonably believes to be necessary for (the child's) proper control, training, or education.' Restatement (Second) of Torts § 147(2) (1965); see id., § 153(2)." At 662: "All of the circumstances are to be taken into account in determining whether the punishment is reasonable in a particular case. Among the most important considerations are the seriousness of the offense, the attitude and past behavior of the child, the nature and severity of the punishment, the age and strength of the child, and the availability of less severe but equally effective means of discipline. Id., at 290-291; Restatement (Second) of Torts § 150, Comments c-e, p. 268 (1965)." The "Id." is 1 F. Harper and F. James, Law of Torts § 3.20 (1956), so the phrase "less severe but equally effective means of discipline" is the Court's summary of Harper and James and of the comments, not the Restatement's own sentence.

Rodney C., 91 Misc. 2d at 680-681, gives the Restatement's own words. Section 150 subdivision (b): "the age, sex, physical and mental condition of the child" are factors. Comment d: a parent is not privileged "to use a means to compel obedience if a less severe method appears likely to be equally effective." Comment e: "a punishment may not be unnecessarily degrading." Section 151: force "applied * * * primarily for any purpose other than proper training or education of the child or for the preservation of discipline is not privileged." Rodney C. is a parental case; Ingraham applies the same sections to teachers through section 147(2) and section 153(2).

How to use: quote Ingraham for the teacher's privilege and for the factor list, and quote Rodney C. when the exact Restatement wording of comment d is wanted. Sacks (2009) at 1174 n.34 reproduces Ingraham's factor list, so her "less severe but equally effective means" is Ingraham's phrase, not the Restatement's. Comment c was not quoted in either opinion and has not been read in this project.

body:

The preceding sentence: "The intent-based executive deprivation model employed in school corporal punishment cases for the past thirty years was rendered unconstitutional nearly two decades ago, but remains the majority rule." Footnote 34 at 1174 quotes Restatement (Second) of Torts section 147(2) and reproduces Ingraham's factor list including "the availability of less severe but equally effective means of discipline," citing section 150 comments c to e. Author then at Texas Southern University, Thurgood Marshall School of Law. Use for the diagnosis that no US court has examined efficacy; the "beyond any reasonable doubt" characterization of the research is the author's and this project's own fact files are more careful about causation.

claim: In Freedom of Religion South Africa v Minister of Justice and Constitutional Development [2019] ZACC 34, decided September 18, 2019, a unanimous Constitutional Court declared the common-law defence of reasonable and moderate parental chastisement unconstitutional, holding at paragraph 70 that 'the paucity of proof that the chastisement is beneficial and the availability of less restrictive means to instil discipline militate against the reasonableness and justification of the limitation.'

sources.title: Freedom of Religion South Africa v Minister of Justice and Constitutional Development and Others (CCT320/17) [2019] ZACC 34; 2019 (11) BCLR 1321 (CC); 2020 (1) SA 1 (CC)
sources.publisher: Southern African Legal Information Institute (full judgment as handed down)

body:
Mogoeng CJ for a unanimous court of ten. The case concerned parents, not schools, and the order (paragraph 76) declares "the common law defence of reasonable and moderate parental chastisement" inconsistent with sections 10 (dignity) and 12(1)(c) (freedom from all forms of violence) of the Constitution. The reasoning that transfers to a necessity argument: paragraph 39, "we must ask why it is necessary to resort to chastisement in the first place. Is it not the actual or potential pain or hurt that flows from it that is believed to be more likely to have a greater effect than any other reasonably available method of discipline?"; paragraph 64, "the paucity of clear or satisfactory empirical evidence that supports chastisement as a beneficial means of instilling discipline"; paragraph 67, force "cannot in circumstances where there is an effective non-violent option available be said to be consonant with the best interests of a child"; paragraph 69, positive parenting "is a less restrictive means of discipline that could potentially be effective in the attainment of the same purpose"; paragraph 70 as quoted in the claim. The court was candid (paragraphs 53, 54 and 64) that some of the research does not separate moderate from abusive force, which is the honest caveat to carry when citing it. The judgment cites the American Academy of Pediatrics 2018 statement (footnote 50).

body:
Each bullet is one account. Quotes are exactly as printed at the URL given; bracketed text is ours. "Permitting state" means the state allowed school corporal punishment at the time of the incident. North Carolina's last districts ended it in 2018; the two NC accounts predate that.

## Former students, recalling it as adults

- **Greg Hooper**, now 31, paddled at 16 at Alvarado High School, Alvarado ISD, Texas, "over a decade ago," for using audio-editing software after finishing his work. Offered in-school suspension or three swats; chose the swats; school phoned his parents first. Verbatim: "He asked me to essentially bend over his desk, and he hit me three times," Hooper told KERA News. "It was humiliating. It was so uncomfortable." And: "He didn't hold back," Hooper said. "It was three full swing hits, and each one hurt more than the last." Source: KERA News, Dylan Duke, 2026-10-12, read at the HPPR republication (URL above). status: verified. Note: KERA's own URL for this story was not located; the HPPR page carries the KERA byline and copyright.

- **Trey Clayton**, 19 at publication, paddled as an 8th grader in March 2011 at Independence High School, Coldwater, Tate County School District, Mississippi, for talking back to a teacher and a librarian; fainted leaving the office after three strikes, breaking his jaw and gashing his chin (court documents). Verbatim: "I'm not going to lie, I was in a lot of trouble during school," Clayton said. "Every time, they gave me the option to get a paddling or get sent home, and I took the paddling." And: "I would go in, get a paddling, come back, go about my day." His mother Dana Hamilton: "When I went to pick him up, my son was spitting teeth into the trash can," she said. Source: Education Week, Sarah D. Sparks, 2016-08-23 (print 2016-08-24). status: verified.

- **Sherrell McGee** (woman), parent and former student, Collins, Covington County School District, Mississippi; paddled as a child and as a high schooler. Verbatim: "I was paddled with a dress on. A dress," she remembers. "Having to bend over, touch the desk, with a dress on. No." Source: The Hechinger Report, Tara García Mathewson, 2022-06-06. status: verified.

- **Damion Rankin Gooden**, 18, paddled in first and second grade at Collins Elementary School, Covington County School District, Mississippi. Verbatim: "You got colors," he explained, "green, yellow, red. Once you get red, you get paddled." Asked whether he was really paddled: "All the time," he said. Source: The Hechinger Report, Tara García Mathewson, 2022-06-06. status: verified.

- **Allison Collins** (girl), senior at Robbinsville High School, Graham County Schools, North Carolina; paddled as a sophomore, her first time in trouble; her father chose the paddle. Verbatim: "That's like my first time ever being in trouble!" And: "And my dad was like, 'Just paddle her.' Because down here in the mountains, we do it the old-school way," Source: WUNC, Jess Clark, 2017-02-23. status: verified. NC permitted at the time; Graham County ended the practice in 2018.

- **Ted Gup**, paddled at 7 in first grade, Belle Stone Elementary School, Canton, Ohio, 1956. Not a permitting state today; included for the sensory detail. Verbatim: "In her strong hands, Mrs. P held a 3-foot-long oak paddle with Greek letters on it — a memento of a college fraternity." "I lurched forward into the wall, stiffening my arms to absorb the shock." "The crack of the paddle resounded down the hall." "I remember limping home over the hill" ... "There were red welts on both cheeks." Source: Salon, Ted Gup (first-person essay), 2001-09-04. status: verified.

## Students interviewed at the time (pseudonyms assigned by HRW/ACLU, 2008)

- **Shannon Q.** (girl), 18, Midland, Texas, interviewed 2008-02-25. Verbatim: "I would have made a different decision if I had known how much it would hurt." Source: HRW/ACLU, A Violent Education, section III, 2008-08. status: verified.

- **LaShell M.** (girl), high school, Mississippi Delta, interviewed 2007-12-04. Verbatim: "He grabs pants to make them tighter on your behind. It hurts more then." Source: same HRW report. status: verified.

- **Matthew S.**, middle school student, Mississippi Delta, interviewed 2007-12-12, describing a paddling in second grade. Verbatim: "It hurt for about two hours, it felt like fire under my butt." Source: same HRW report. status: verified.

## Parents, on the record, under their own names

- **Linda Pee**, mother of **Audrey** (girl), East Webster High School, Webster County School District, Mississippi. Audrey paddled first in sixth grade (one lick from the gym coach, lined up with 10 tardy students, in front of the class; purple bruises, ER visit) and again in March 2007 in twelfth grade (two blows from the principal in his office, for sweatpants that showed her ankles) after her mother had opted her out in writing. Verbatim: "The paddles they use look sort of like a flattened baseball bat – they're a piece of wood about 15 inches long, three inches wide, and an inch thick, with a handle at one end." And: "She said the principal would leave the door open so people could see that he was hitting people." And: "She was paddled in first period and she had bruises all over her by third period." Source: written testimony to the US House Education and Labor subcommittee, 2010-04-15 (PDF, read with pdftotext). status: verified. Note: these are the mother's words; the PDF attributes no direct quote to Audrey.

- **Tessa Davis**, mother, Arkansas (school outside Little Rock, unnamed); chose paddling for her son "C" in kindergarten about eight years ago (he is 13 now). Verbatim: "I was kind of at, just like my breaking point," Davis recalled. "And he was like, 'Well, I was paddled, so give him the paddling.'" "So that's what we chose." "And I just remember feeling like instant regret." Source: NPR, Kadin Mills, 2026-08-20, read at the KCUR republication. status: verified.

- **Venus Maynor**, father of **Orrie**, paddled in second grade at Prospect Elementary School, Public Schools of Robeson County, North Carolina, for running out of line in the hall. Verbatim: "She said 'Hey we're going to paddle you for not doing what we asked you to do'," he said. "And of course she made good on her promise. She paddled him when they got back to the room with a witness." Source: WUNC, Jess Clark, 2017-02-23. status: verified.

## Educators who administered it, or refused to

- **Chris Belcher**, now assistant teaching professor, MU College of Education and Human Development, former Columbia Public Schools superintendent, Missouri. In the 1980s, early in his administrative career, he was told to paddle a special-education student because the administrator who normally handled that student was absent. Verbatim: "The kid screamed, and I felt awful," he said. (The article's "worst experience of his life" is paraphrase.) Source: Columbia Missourian, Sofi Zeman, 2023-04-03, read at The 74 republication (Missouri Independent page returned 403). status: verified.

- **Ralph McClaney**, assistant principal, Carver Middle School, Meridian Public School District, Mississippi; resigned 2003-09-30 rather than paddle a sixth-grade girl on the principal's order. Verbatim: "The idea of a big white guy hitting an 80-pound black girl because she talked back to the teacher did not sit well with me," and "I decided I did not get my master's degree in education to spend my time paddling students." Source: The Washington Post, Michael Dobbs, 2004-02-22, read at The Seattle Times archive. status: verified.

- **Alan Gordon**, elementary principal, Warner Public Schools, Oklahoma, who still administers paddlings (two paddles named "Peace" and "Harmony"). Verbatim: "The shop teacher made my paddles for me," said Gordon. "I sit right here before I even spank them." "They place their hands flat on the desk, they look at the picture and they spread their legs apart." Source: NPR, Kadin Mills, 2026-08-20, read at the KCUR republication. status: verified. Useful as the administrator's-eye view; he defends the practice.
